title: The Mental Health Act 1983 and its Code of Practice
blurb: Define mental disorder, name the key MHA roles and apply the Code's five guiding principles.
question: Kofi, a newly registered mental health nurse, is asked by a student how the Mental Health Act 1983 decides who it covers and which professional usually makes an application for detention. What should Kofi explain?

teach.h: What the Mental Health Act does
teach.body: The Mental Health Act 1983 (as amended in 2007) is the law in England and Wales that allows people with a mental disorder to be assessed, detained and treated in hospital, or supervised in the community, without their consent when strict criteria are met. In plain English: it is the legal safety net for when someone is too unwell to keep themselves or others safe and will not accept help voluntarily. The 2015 Code of Practice explains how to use it well.
teach.cite: Mental Health Act 1983 (as amended); Code of Practice 2015, s118

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Any disorder or disability of the mind
Alcohol or drug dependence alone is not a mental disorder
Needs abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct for s3, CTO and renewal (not s2)
Must be available for s3, a CTO and renewal
Includes nursing, psychological intervention and rehabilitation
teach.caption: One broad definition replaced the old four categories of mental disorder in 2008.
AMHPs are social workers, mental health or learning disability nurses, occupational therapists or chartered psychologists; a doctor cannot be an AMHP (s114(2)).

letters.word: Least restrictive option and maximising independence

teach.caption: All five are of equal importance and should inform every decision under the Act (COP15 1.23).

teach.body: The Code of Practice is issued under s118 of the Act. Professionals must have regard to it, and anyone who departs from the Code or a guiding principle should document and justify that decision; the Care Quality Commission looks for this evidence. Lawful decisions must also comply with the Human Rights Act 1998 and the Equality Act 2010. The 2015 Code is still the current Code.

steps.label: NR consulted

teach.body: Kofi tells the student that the Act covers any disorder or disability of the mind, but not alcohol or drug dependence on its own. Most applications are made by an AMHP rather than the nearest relative, because the Code sees the AMHP as better placed and it protects family relationships (COP15 14.30). The responsible clinician then leads treatment. Kofi adds that every decision should reflect the five guiding principles, recorded in the notes.

teach.text: Three sets of principles get mixed up. The Code's FIVE guiding principles (least restrictive, empowerment, respect, purpose, efficiency) apply now. The MCA's five principles (presume capacity and so on) are a different Act. The Mental Health Act 2025's four principles (choice and autonomy, least restriction, therapeutic benefit, person as an individual) are enacted but NOT yet in force.

items: Mental disorder = any disorder or disability of the mind; dependence alone does not count.
Learning disability alone: s2 is possible, but s3 needs abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct.
AMHP usually applies; the RC leads treatment; the NR has powers to apply, object and seek discharge.
The 2015 Code's five guiding principles are of equal weight; document and justify any departure.

summary: You can now define mental disorder under the Act, explain the roles of the AMHP, responsible clinician and nearest relative, and apply the Code's five guiding principles. You can also tell these principles apart from the MCA principles and the not-yet-commenced 2025 Act principles.

A.q: A student asks how the Mental Health Act 1983, as amended, defines mental disorder. Which answer is accurate?
options: A psychotic or mood disorder of moderate severity
Any condition listed in ICD-11 chapter 6
Any disorder or disability of the mind
A mental illness needing in-patient treatment
A.why: Section 1(2) defines mental disorder as any disorder or disability of the mind. It is one broad definition, not a list of diagnoses.

whyNot.0: The Act sets no diagnostic group or severity threshold in its definition.
whyNot.1: The Act does not import a clinical classification such as ICD-11.
whyNot.3: Whether in-patient treatment is needed belongs to the section criteria, not the definition.

A.q: Which presentation, on its own, falls outside the definition of mental disorder in the Act?
A.why: Section 1(3) states that dependence on alcohol or drugs is not considered a disorder or disability of the mind for the purposes of the definition.

whyNot.1: Learning disability is a mental disorder; it carries an extra conduct requirement for s3 and other longer-term powers.
whyNot.2: Eating disorders are disorders of the mind within s1(2).
whyNot.3: Personality disorders fall within the broad s1(2) definition.

A.q: Which of these is one of the five guiding principles in the 2015 Mental Health Act Code of Practice?
A.why: Purpose and effectiveness is one of the Code's five guiding principles, alongside least restrictive option, empowerment and involvement, respect and dignity, and efficiency and equity.

whyNot.0: Therapeutic benefit is one of the four principles in the Mental Health Act 2025, which are not yet in force.
whyNot.2: Presumption of capacity is a Mental Capacity Act 2005 principle.
whyNot.3: Choice and autonomy is a 2025 Act principle that has not been commenced.

B.q: Mr Hussain's daughter is his nearest relative. She asks whether she should make the application to detain him herself. What does the Code of Practice advise?
options: The responsible clinician should make it
A relative applicant is preferred by the Code
The GP should apply after examining him
An AMHP is usually the better applicant
B.why: COP15 14.30: an AMHP is usually more appropriate than the nearest relative, given their training, and it avoids harming the family relationship.

whyNot.0: Only an AMHP or the nearest relative can apply under Part 2; the RC is not an applicant.
whyNot.1: The Code prefers the AMHP, partly to protect the relationship between patient and relative.
whyNot.2: A doctor gives a medical recommendation, not the application.

B.q: Ellis, 22, has a learning disability and no other mental disorder. There is no abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct. Which power could still be used if its criteria are met?
options: A community treatment order under section 17A
B.why: The learning disability conduct qualification applies to s3, s17A, s20 and other longer-term powers, but not to s2 assessment.

whyNot.0: Section 3 needs the learning disability to be associated with abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct.
whyNot.2: A CTO is within the list of powers needing the conduct qualification.
whyNot.3: Renewal under s20 also needs the conduct qualification.

B.q: For which power must appropriate medical treatment be available for the patient?
B.why: The appropriate medical treatment test is part of the s3 criteria (s3(2)(d)) and also applies to CTOs and renewals.

whyNot.0: Section 2 is for assessment and has no appropriate medical treatment test.
whyNot.1: Section 5(2) holds an in-patient while an application is considered; it has no such test.
whyNot.3: Section 4 is an emergency assessment route without that test.

C.q: A ward manager wants to adopt a local practice that differs from a recommendation in the Mental Health Act Code of Practice. What is the correct position?
options: It needs approval from the nearest relative
The decision should be documented and justified
The ward manager may decide this without recording it
The Code binds staff as strictly as the Act
C.why: The Code is statutory guidance. COP15 1.24 says any decision to depart from it should be documented and justified, and the CQC looks for this.

whyNot.0: Nearest relatives have specific statutory powers; approving policy departures is not one of them.
whyNot.2: COP15 1.24 requires any departure from the Code to be documented and justified, so an unrecorded local decision is not enough.
whyNot.3: The Code is not the Act itself; justified departures are possible.

C.q: The team invites Sara, who is detained, and her chosen carer to help write her care plan, and records Sara's views where they differ from the team's. Which guiding principle is this most directly applying?
options: Least restrictive option and maximising independence
C.why: Involving the patient and carers in planning, and recording the patient's views, is the empowerment and involvement principle.

whyNot.0: Efficiency and equity is about fair, well-used resources and timely access.
whyNot.1: Purpose and effectiveness is about evidence-based care with clear goals.
whyNot.2: Least restrictive option is about minimising restrictions and maximising independence.

C.q: Mr Price is on a planned alcohol detoxification ward. He has no other mental disorder, is not intoxicated and wants to leave. A colleague suggests using the Mental Health Act. What is the correct position?
options: Section 5(4) applies as he is an in-patient
Section 2 applies because dependence is a mental disorder
Dependence alone does not bring him within the Act
C.why: Section 1(3): dependence on alcohol or drugs is not a disorder or disability of the mind, so the Act cannot be used on that basis alone.

whyNot.0: Section 5(4) needs a mental disorder and a patient receiving treatment for mental disorder.
whyNot.1: The Act expressly excludes dependence alone from the definition.
whyNot.2: Section 3 also needs a mental disorder within the definition.

reteach.title: Who, what and how
reteach.question: Think of the Act as answering three questions: who does it cover, who uses it, and how should they use it?

blocks.body: WHO: anyone with a disorder or disability of the mind (not dependence alone). WHO USES IT: usually an AMHP applies with two medical recommendations; the responsible clinician then leads treatment; the nearest relative has safeguarding powers. HOW: guided by the Code's five principles, with any departure documented and justified.

items.label: AMHP must have seen the person before applying
medical recommendations for s2 or s3

blocks.text: Learning disability is a mental disorder, but s3, CTOs and renewals need abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct. Section 2 does not.

explain.body: Mental disorder means any disorder or disability of the mind (s1(2)). Dependence on alcohol or drugs alone is excluded (s1(3)). A learning disability counts, but longer-term powers need the conduct qualification.

test.q: Which statement about the definition of mental disorder is correct?
options: It lists four legal categories of disorder
test.why: Section 1(3) excludes dependence on alcohol or drugs alone from the definition.

whyNot.1: Personality disorder falls within any disorder or disability of the mind.
whyNot.2: The four categories were replaced by one definition in 2008.
whyNot.3: Learning disability is included, with a conduct qualification for longer-term powers.

explain.body: The AMHP usually makes the application after interviewing the person (s13(2)) and informing (s2) or consulting (s3) the nearest relative (s11(3)-(4)). The responsible clinician is the approved clinician with overall responsibility for the patient's case. The nearest relative can apply, object to s3 and order discharge.

test.q: Which professional cannot act as an approved mental health professional?
test.why: AMHPs come from social work, nursing, occupational therapy and psychology; doctors give the medical recommendations instead.

whyNot.0: Mental health and learning disability nurses can be approved as AMHPs.
whyNot.1: Social workers are the largest group of AMHPs.
whyNot.3: Occupational therapists can be approved as AMHPs.

explain.body: Least restrictive option and maximising independence; empowerment and involvement; respect and dignity; purpose and effectiveness; efficiency and equity. They are of equal importance, balanced case by case.

test.q: How do the Code's five guiding principles relate to each other?
options: Least restrictive option overrides the rest
Respect and dignity is ranked first
Efficiency and equity applies to managers
test.why: COP15 1.23: all five sets of principles are of equal importance, with the weight balanced according to the circumstances.

whyNot.0: No principle overrides the others; they are balanced.
whyNot.2: The Code does not rank the principles.
whyNot.3: All principles apply to everyone making decisions under the Act.

explain.body: The Code is statutory guidance under s118. Decisions to depart from it should be documented and justified. Lawful decisions also comply with the Human Rights Act 1998 and Equality Act 2010.

test.q: Under which section of the Mental Health Act 1983 is the Code of Practice issued?
test.why: Section 118 requires the Secretary of State to prepare and publish the Code of Practice.

whyNot.0: Section 132 is the duty to give detained patients information.
whyNot.2: Section 136 is the police power to remove a person to a place of safety.
